title: A2 Review: The Four Tenses
subtitle: Present simple, present continuous, past simple and the future — what each one is actually for.
description: An A2 review reading and listening text explaining when to use each of the four core tenses, with practice exercises on all of them.
passage: Most students at this level already know how to build the four main tenses. What is harder is knowing which one a sentence needs, and that is usually decided by the time word, not by the verb.

The present simple is for things that are generally true, and for habits. I work in a hospital. She goes to bed at half past ten. We do not like coffee. The words that go with it are always, usually, often, sometimes, never, every day, on Saturdays. If you can put “every week” into the sentence without it sounding strange, you probably want the present simple.

The present continuous is for right now, or for a period around now. Be quiet — the baby is sleeping. Look! It is raining. I am reading a very long book at the moment. Its words are now, right now, at the moment, today, and the imperatives look and listen, which almost always introduce it. Notice the difference: “He works in a hospital” is his job, and “He is working on Saturday” is this weekend only.

The past simple is for finished actions at a finished time. We went to the lake last Saturday. She did not come to the party. The time word — yesterday, last week, in 2019, two days ago — is what forces it, and once that word is in the sentence no other tense is possible. The difficulty is not the rule but the verbs: about half of the common ones are irregular and simply have to be learned. Went, saw, took, ran, swam, caught, bought, brought.

For the future, English gives you three options and they are not interchangeable. Use will for a decision made as you speak, or a prediction: I will help you with that. It will rain tomorrow. Use going to for an intention you already had: I am going to look for a new job. And use the present continuous for something already arranged, usually with another person: I am meeting Sarah at six. The last one surprises learners, because it looks like the present.

One last thing that causes trouble. Some verbs do not normally take the continuous, even when you are talking about this moment: know, want, like, need, understand, believe. You say I know the answer, never I am knowing the answer, and this is one of the few places where English is stricter than most languages.

vocabulary.definition: to put a sentence or a form together
something you do regularly, usually without thinking
a word such as yesterday or always that shows when something happens
to feel wrong to a native speaker, even if the grammar is correct
a command form such as look or listen
able to be used in place of one another
to fix something in advance with somebody else

exercises.title: Present Simple or Present Continuous?
exercises.instructions: Look for the time word first. Simple for habits, continuous for now.

items.prompt: Right now she ___ English in the library.
items.explanation: “Right now” makes it continuous.

items.prompt: My brother usually ___ football on Saturdays.
items.explanation: “Usually” and “on Saturdays” both mark a habit.

items.prompt: Be quiet! The baby ___.
items.explanation: The command “be quiet” shows it is happening at this moment.

items.prompt: We ___ TV very often.
items.explanation: “Very often” is a frequency word, so present simple — and “we” takes don't, not doesn't.

items.prompt: Look! It ___ outside.
items.explanation: “Look!” almost always introduces the present continuous.

items.prompt: What ___ you ___ at the moment?
items.explanation: A question in the present continuous: are + subject + -ing.

items.prompt: I ___ the answer to that question.
items.explanation: Know is one of the verbs that does not take the continuous, whatever the time.

exercises.title: Past Simple
exercises.instructions: Every sentence has a finished past time. Watch for the irregular verbs.

items.prompt: Last weekend we ___ to the lake and ___ in the water.
items.explanation: Two irregulars: go → went, swim → swam.

items.prompt: She ___ to the party because she ___ ill.
items.explanation: After didn't the verb returns to its base form: didn't come, never didn't came.

items.prompt: I ___ that film two years ago and I ___ it.
items.explanation: One irregular and one regular in the same sentence — English mixes them constantly.

items.prompt: ___ you ___ the tickets yesterday?
items.explanation: In a question, did carries the past and the main verb stays in the base form.

items.prompt: He ___ his keys and ___ them under the sofa.
items.explanation: Lose → lost and find → found. Both are on the list worth memorising.

exercises.title: Three Futures
exercises.instructions: Will for a decision now or a prediction. Going to for an intention you already had. Present continuous for something arranged with someone.

items.prompt: That bag looks heavy. I ___ ___ you.
items.explanation: The decision is made at the moment of speaking, so will.

items.prompt: I ___ ___ ___ look for a new job next year.
items.explanation: An intention the speaker already had before this conversation.

items.prompt: I ___ Sarah at six — we agreed yesterday.
items.explanation: Already arranged with another person, so the present continuous. This is the one learners least expect.

items.prompt: Look at those clouds. It ___ ___.
items.explanation: Going to is used for a prediction you can see the evidence for right now.

items.prompt: What does the text say usually decides which tense a sentence needs?
options: The time word, not the verb
Whether the sentence is positive or negative
items.explanation: Which is why every exercise above starts by asking you to find the time word.

items.prompt: What is the test the writer gives for the present simple?
options: Whether “every week” can be added without sounding strange
Whether the sentence has a subject
items.explanation: A quick practical test for whether something is a habit.

items.prompt: What is the difference between “He works on Saturday” and “He is working on Saturday”?
options: The first is his job; the second is this weekend only
items.explanation: General truth against temporary arrangement — the same contrast the whole text is built on.

items.prompt: What does the writer say is the real difficulty with the past simple?
options: The irregular verbs, about half of the common ones
items.explanation: “The difficulty is not the rule but the verbs… and simply have to be learned.”

items.prompt: Why does the writer say the third future “surprises learners”?
options: It looks like the present, but refers to the future
items.explanation: “I am meeting Sarah at six” has present form and future meaning.

discussion: Say three things you do every week, and three things you are doing this week.
What did you do last weekend? Use five past simple verbs, and try to include two irregular ones.
Say one thing you will do, one you are going to do, and one you are doing — and explain why each takes that form.
Which of the four tenses is hardest for you? What goes wrong?
Write about 100 words about your week: what you usually do, what you are doing now, and what you will do next.
